hook: A bakery sells more croissants on Monday because it cut the price. On Tuesday it sells more again, at the old price, because an office opened next door. Both days end with more croissants sold, yet the graphs look different: on Monday buyers moved along the curve, and on Tuesday the whole curve moved. Telling these two apart is one of the most tested graph skills in the course.

ideas: Each curve holds everything except its two graphed variables constant ("other things equal").
A change in a variable on one of the axes is a movement along a curve: a new point, the same curve.
A change in anything else is a shift of a curve: the whole curve moves to a new position.
A shift right means a larger quantity at every price; a shift left means a smaller quantity at every price. Say "right" or "left", not "up" or "down".
Draw a shift so it scores: old curve with subscript 1, new curve with subscript 2, an arrow from old to new.

misconception.wrong: The bakery cut its price and sold more croissants, so the curve D shifted right.
misconception.right: Price is on the vertical axis, so a price cut moves buyers down along the same curve D to a larger quantity. D shifts only when something other than the croissant's own price changes.

summary: A curve on a market graph shows how quantity relates to price with everything else held equal. When the good's own price changes, the market moves along the same curve to a new point. When anything else changes, such as buyers' incomes, sellers' costs or the number of buyers, the whole curve shifts: right for a larger quantity at every price, left for a smaller one. Show a shift with the old curve labeled 1, the new curve labeled 2 and an arrow between them.
